(CNN) -- Legendary singer-songwriter Aretha Franklin performed "My Country 'Tis of Thee" at Tuesday's inauguration. Franklin has since remarked that the cold weather affected her voice during the performance. CNN's Larry King spoke with "The Queen of Soul" about the significance of the nation's first black president, her experience singing at the inauguration, and the much-discussed hat she wore.

**Larry King:** Where did you get that hat?

**Aretha Franklin:** I purchased it at a small millinery shop that I frequent in Detroit.

**King:** What was Tuesday like for you?

**Franklin:** Oh, what a tremendous, monumental day. From the morning through the evening, and the ball—every event, one after another—it was simply overwhelming.

**King:** How did you learn that you would be singing?

**Franklin:** My agent called to inform me that he had received both an invitation and a telephone call requesting my presence and performance at the swearing-in and the inauguration.

**King:** Did you select the song yourself?

**Franklin:** Yes, I did.

**King:** Is it a difficult song to sing?

**Franklin:** Not at all—though on Tuesday it certainly was, largely because of the outdoor temperature. As you well know, if you were there, it was freezing. Some singers are unaffected by the cold, while others are not. I am not fond of it, and it took a toll on my voice.

*Watch Franklin sing at inauguration »*

**King:** You sang at Martin Luther King's funeral. What do you remember about that?

**Franklin:** There were, of course, very long lines. I recall walking in the street behind the bier, perhaps 200 or 300 feet away from it. I remember that Leontyne Price was there, as was Eartha Kitt. We were shuttled from one location to another. The passing of a great man was upon us.

**King:** How did you feel yesterday, witnessing a young black man elected president?

**Franklin:** Oh, how does one put it into words? There is a genuine love affair unfolding between the country and Barack. I believe this is the age of Barack—people have simply fallen head over heels in love with him. His ascent to the presidency was nothing short of miraculous. Yet we must remember that he cannot perform miracles overnight. It will take time.

*Watch Franklin discuss the joy of seeing the nation's first black president »*

There are a great many problems, and a wealth of challenges for him and his administration to address.

**King:** With your magnificent voice, is it difficult to sing outdoors?

**Franklin:** It depends on the temperature. Yesterday, Mother Nature was not very kind to me—and I intend to have a word with her when I return home. It was by no means up to my usual standard, and I was not pleased with it. Still, I feel blessed, because it could have been five above or five below zero, as it often is in Detroit. I was fortunate enough to at least carry the melody, though I was not entirely happy with the result.

**King:** It was wonderful to hear.

**Franklin:** I was delighted and thrilled to be there. That was what mattered most—not so much the performance itself, but simply being present to witness this great man take office, and to see the promise of tomorrow come to pass.

# Aretha Franklin: A Legendary Voice Remembered

When CNN and news outlets around the world announced the passing of Aretha Franklin in August 2018, the tributes poured in from every corner of the globe. The world had lost not just a singer, but a true legend whose voice defined generations.

## The Queen of Soul

Aretha Franklin earned her title as the "Queen of Soul" through decades of unforgettable music. Her powerful voice carried hits like "Respect," "Chain of Fools," and "(You Make Me Feel Like) A Natural Woman" into the hearts of millions. These weren't just songs—they became anthems that transcended the music charts to influence culture, civil rights, and the very definition of American artistry.

## A Legendary Career

What made Aretha truly legendary was her remarkable range and emotional depth. Born in Memphis in 1942 and raised in Detroit, she began singing in her father's church before rising to international stardom. Over her career, she earned 18 Grammy Awards and became the first woman inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1987.

CNN's extensive coverage of her life highlighted not only her musical achievements but also her role as a symbol of empowerment. Her rendition of "Respect" became an unofficial anthem for both the civil rights and women's movements.

## An Enduring Legacy

News networks like CNN continue to celebrate Aretha's contributions long after her passing. Her performances at historic events—including singing at President Barack Obama's inauguration—cemented her place in history.

Aretha Franklin's legendary status isn't measured only by awards or record sales, but by the way her music continues to inspire artists and move listeners across the world. The Queen of Soul may be gone, but her voice remains eternal.

counterfactuals.output:
**CNN LARRY KING LIVE**

*Aired January 2009*

**BEGIN TRANSCRIPT**

**LARRY KING, HOST:** Good evening. What a moment we all witnessed this week. The inauguration of Barack Obama, the 44th President of the United States, and the first African American to hold that office. And there, singing in the cold on the steps of the Capitol, one of the greatest voices this country has ever produced. She is the Queen of Soul. Aretha Franklin joins us tonight. It's always a thrill, Aretha. Welcome.

**ARETHA FRANKLIN, SINGER:** Thank you, Larry. It's wonderful to be here with you.

**KING:** Let's start with the obvious. What was it like to stand up there and sing at that inauguration?

**FRANKLIN:** Oh, Larry, it was one of the greatest honors of my life. To be a part of history like that — I don't think I've ever felt anything quite like it. You look out and you see this ocean of people, all these faces, and you feel the weight of the moment. It was overwhelming, in the best way.

**KING:** You sang "My Country, 'Tis of Thee."

**FRANKLIN:** I did. And that song means so much, especially on a day like that day. "Let freedom ring." Standing there, singing those words, with the first African American president about to take the oath — it just took on a whole new meaning for me.

**KING:** Now I have to ask you about the hat. That hat became a sensation. People are talking about it all over the world.

**FRANKLIN:** *(laughs)* The hat! Oh, I've never gotten so much attention for a hat in my whole life. It's taken on a life of its own, Larry.

**KING:** Tell me about it. Where did it come from?

**FRANKLIN:** Well, I have a wonderful milliner in Detroit, and we designed it together. I wanted something special, something that felt right for the occasion. That gray felt with the big bow and the rhinestones. I loved it. I had no idea it would become such a thing.

**KING:** There are Facebook pages, people putting that hat on everything.

**FRANKLIN:** I've heard! They've been putting my hat on the Mona Lisa, on all kinds of things. I think it's just delightful. If people are having fun with it, then I'm happy about that.

**KING:** Now the weather. It was bitterly cold that day. Does cold weather affect a singer's voice?

**FRANKLIN:** Oh, absolutely it does, Larry. Cold air is very hard on the vocal cords. Your throat tightens up, you can't warm up the way you'd like to. It was, what, in the twenties out there with the wind? A singer wants warmth. You want to be able to relax those muscles.

**KING:** So it was a challenge.

**FRANKLIN:** It was a challenge. I'll be honest with you. It wasn't the performance I would have given in a warm concert hall. But you do the best you can under the circumstances, and I gave it everything I had that day. When you're singing for history, you find a way.

**KING:** Would you have done anything differently?

**FRANKLIN:** *(laughs)* Maybe asked for a heater! No, I have no regrets. It was a blessing to be there.

**KING:** Let me ask you about the bigger picture. What does it mean to you, personally, to see a black president take office?

**FRANKLIN:** Larry, I never thought I would live to see this day. I marched in the movement. I remember Dr. King. My father was a minister, and he was very active, and we knew Dr. King personally. He came to our home. And to think of everything this country has been through, all the struggle and the sacrifice, and now to see this — it moves me to tears.

**KING:** You knew Dr. King.

**FRANKLIN:** I did. And I kept thinking about him that day. I kept thinking, if only he could see this. All those people who came before, who fought and gave their lives, they made this possible. President Obama is standing on their shoulders. We all are.

**KING:** What are your hopes for this presidency?

**FRANKLIN:** My hope is that he brings people together. This is a young man with a good heart and a good mind, and I believe he's going to do great things. I pray for him. These are hard times, and he's got a big job ahead of him. But I have faith. That day gave a lot of people hope, and hope is a powerful thing.

**KING:** Aretha Franklin, the Queen of Soul. Always a pleasure. Thank you for being here.

**FRANKLIN:** Thank you, Larry. Bless you.

**KING:** We'll be right back.

**END TRANSCRIPT**

*(This is a fictional transcript created for illustrative purposes, dramatizing real events from the January 2009 inauguration.)*

*By CNN Entertainment Staff*

In an exclusive conversation following her stirring inaugural performance, the legendary Aretha Franklin joined Larry King for an intimate discussion about music, history, and the honor of singing for the nation.

---

**LARRY KING:** Aretha, thank you for being here. You just performed at the presidential inauguration. What was going through your mind up on that stage?

**ARETHA FRANKLIN:** Larry, it's such a pleasure. You know, standing up there, looking out at all those faces, all those flags—I felt the weight of history. I thought about my father, about the church where I first sang, about every road that led me to this moment. It was humbling.

**KING:** You've performed for presidents before. Does it ever get routine?

**FRANKLIN:** *(laughs)* Never routine, Larry. Never. Every time is like the first time. When you're singing for the country, you're not just singing notes. You're carrying people's hopes, their dreams. That's a responsibility I take very seriously.

**KING:** Let's talk about the song choice. Tell me about that.

**FRANKLIN:** Well, I wanted something that would speak to everyone—no matter who they voted for, no matter where they come from. Music has a way of bringing people together when nothing else can. That's always been my mission, going back to the civil rights days.

**KING:** You mentioned the civil rights movement. You were there, alongside Dr. King. How does a day like today connect to that struggle?

**FRANKLIN:** Larry, days like this are the dream made real. We marched. We sang. We believed. And to stand on that platform today, to be part of this peaceful transfer of power in front of the whole world—it tells me we're still moving forward. Not fast enough sometimes, but forward.

**KING:** The hat, Aretha. I have to ask about the hat. It's already all over the news.

**FRANKLIN:** *(laughs heartily)* Oh, the hat! You know, a woman's got to make an entrance. I told my milliner, make it special, make it a showstopper. Looks like it did its job, didn't it?

**KING:** It certainly did. People are already talking about selling replicas.

**FRANKLIN:** Well, if they do, I want my cut! *(laughs)*

**KING:** After all these decades, all the awards, all the honors—what keeps you singing?

**FRANKLIN:** The love, Larry. The love between me and the audience. When I open my mouth and the people respond, there's nothing like it in this world. As long as the good Lord gives me breath, I'll keep singing.

**KING:** Any advice for young artists watching today?

**FRANKLIN:** Respect yourself. Know your worth. And never forget where you came from. The music industry will try to change you, but your gift is yours. Guard it. Nurture it. And always, always sing from your heart.

**KING:** Aretha Franklin, the Queen of Soul. It's been an honor.

**FRANKLIN:** The honor is mine, Larry. God bless.

---

*In the style of a Larry King interview*

**LARRY KING:** We're here tonight with a living legend, an artist whose voice has become part of the American soundtrack. The Queen of Soul herself. Thank you for being here.

**ARETHA FRANKLIN:** Larry, it's always a pleasure. You know I love talking with you.

**KING:** *(laughs)* Before we go—after all these years, all these honors, what keeps you singing?

**FRANKLIN:** Love, Larry. It's always been love. The music is how I love this world. And as long as I have breath in me, I'm going to keep on giving it.

When Aretha Franklin took the stage on January 20, 2009, to sing "My Country 'Tis of Thee" at Barack Obama's inauguration, millions watched—and one detail became almost as memorable as the performance itself: that hat. But behind the now-iconic gray bow was a singer battling brutal Washington cold. We sat down to talk about the day.

---

**Q: Let's start with the weather. It was famously freezing that morning.**

Oh, it was bitter. People don't understand what cold does to a voice. Your vocal cords, your breath control—everything tightens up. I'm a woman who takes her instrument seriously, and I could feel it fighting me out there. The temperature was down in the twenties, and you're sitting, waiting, and by the time you rise to sing, your body just isn't warm the way it needs to be.

**Q: Did you feel the performance suffered because of it?**

I'll be honest with you—it wasn't my best. I know what I'm capable of, and the cold took something from me that day. You want to give the people everything, especially on a day like that. But when your body is that cold, you're managing it note by note. I would have loved to sing it in a warm hall. I think folks would have heard something different.

**Q: And yet the moment clearly meant something bigger.**

That's just it. Whatever the cold did to those notes, it couldn't touch what that day *was*. I've lived through a lot in this country. I marched, I sang in churches, I knew Dr. King. To stand there and watch a young Black man raise his hand and become President of the United States—I never let myself believe I'd see it.

**Q: What went through your mind watching him take the oath?**

I thought about my father, Reverend Franklin, and all the ministers and marchers who didn't live to see it. I thought about the years of struggle, the people who gave everything. And here was this brilliant young man, dignified, with his beautiful family beside him. I felt joy, but I also felt the weight of history sitting on my shoulders. It was almost too much to hold.

**Q: Was there pride in being part of it?**

Enormous pride. However that song came out, I was *there*. I got to lend my voice to that page in history. That's a blessing I'll carry the rest of my days. The hat got all the attention—[laughs]—but I'll tell you, I felt something spiritual up on that platform. Cold and all.

**Q: Any final thoughts on that day?**

Just gratitude. This country made me work for every inch, but it gave me that morning. A Black man in the White House. Chosen by the people. Whatever else I remember, I'll remember standing in the cold, watching the future open up.

---

*The Queen of Soul remains, as ever, unbowed—hat or no hat.*
